name: The First 90 Days
title: The First 90 Days
answer: The First 90 Days is a starting plan for superintendents, principals, teachers, and parents who want to begin using AI in schools without buying new technology. It matters because it turns a vague question about where to start into a short set of concrete moves for each role, focused on governance, people, practice, and understanding.

sections.body: The First 90 Days addresses the common question from leaders and families about where to begin with AI in a school. It offers a separate starting list for four roles: superintendent, principal, teacher, and parent. Each list draws on the Thirty Day Moves described elsewhere in the volume, so the plan is cumulative rather than a new set of demands. None of the moves requires purchasing new technology, which keeps the focus on decisions and habits rather than products. The idea solves the problem of scattered, role-blind advice by giving each person a clear and bounded first step.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: For a superintendent, the first 90 days focus on governance and modeling: publishing the approved tool list and the human review rule, using AI visibly in their own work, choosing one pilot with a clear measure and a comparison group, and reporting results to the board including what did not work. For a principal, the focus is people and time: naming an AI champion, running a small time study with volunteers, deciding with teachers where saved time will go, checking that every tool in the building is approved, and sharing learning with staff and families. For a teacher, the focus is practice and habits: trying AI for one planning task and one feedback task while checking every output, labeling assignments with AI use levels, building revision into class time, and keeping student names and work out of unapproved tools. For a parent, the focus is understanding: asking the school the five questions from Chapter 14, talking with their child about AI use and asking them to explain their work, attending a parent AI night if offered, and sharing what they learn with other families. The text does not give separate grade bands for these moves.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not present a study, figure, or formal evidence label for the First 90 Days. It describes the plan as drawing on the Thirty Day Moves throughout the volume and as a practical starting point for each role. No research finding is cited for the plan itself, so this idea rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets limits that keep decisions with people rather than tools. Superintendents must publish the approved tool list and the human review rule, and they must report results to the board including what did not work. Principals must confirm that every AI tool in the building is on the approved list and must decide with teachers where saved time will go. Teachers must check every output, label assignments with AI use levels, build revision into class time, and keep student names and work out of any tool not on the approved list. Parents are directed to ask the school the five questions from Chapter 14 and to talk with their child about how they use AI and to explain their work.
